vignette:
He was fifty-four when it happened, though in our sessions he speaks of it as if it were yesterday. Rajesh works for a small non-profit that resettles refugees, a job he took after retiring from a decades-long career in accounting. He tells me he chose the work because he wanted to give back, to help people whose lives had been shattered by violence. He never expected that the work would stir up his own wreckage.

The trauma occurred fourteen years ago, during a business trip to a city he won't name. He had stayed late at a conference, and on his walk back to the hotel, he was followed into a narrow alley. A man, then another, cornered him. They beat him and they raped him. Rajesh remembers the smell of damp concrete, the weight of a knee on his chest, the sound of his own breath trapped in his throat. He did not report it to the police. He did not tell his wife. He flew home the next morning and went back to his desk. In his mind, he tells me, it was not the kind of thing that happened to men like him-a husband, a father, a professional. He convinced himself it was a mugging gone wrong, an unfortunate incident. He buried it.

The symptoms did not stay buried. Two years later, his wife left him. She said he had become distant, irritable, unreachable. He could not explain the nights he woke drenched in sweat, or the way he flinched when a colleague touched his shoulder. He started drinking in the evenings, alone, to quiet the rage that flared without warning. He lost interest in the things that once gave him pleasure-cooking, reading, weekend walks. He began avoiding crowds, then public transport, then any situation where he might feel trapped. He would take the stairs instead of an elevator, even when his knees ached. He would scan a restaurant for exits before sitting down. He told himself he was just getting older, more cautious.

Now, at sixty-eight, the world has shrunk to a narrow radius: his apartment, the non-profit office, a grocery store he visits at 7 a.m. to avoid the rush. He works with refugees, many of whom have survived sexual violence in detention centers or war zones. He listens to their stories with an unbearable empathy. Sometimes, during an intake interview, a client will describe being held down, and Rajesh will feel the floor tilt beneath him. He will excuse himself to the restroom, brace his hands on the sink, and wait for the shaking to stop. He has developed a habit of washing his hands three times after each meeting-not for hygiene, but because it is the only thing that makes the dirt on his skin go away.

At night, he cannot lie on his back. He sleeps curled on his side, facing the door. He keeps a lamp on. His therapist-our sessions began three months ago, after a colleague noticed his trembling hands during a staff meeting-has asked him about intimacy. He has not had a romantic partner since the divorce. He says he does not miss it. But the truth, which he whispered last week, is that he cannot bear to be touched. The last time someone hugged him, at a holiday party, he felt the alley walls close in again.

He speaks of his body as a betrayal. It feels foreign to him, fragile, marked. He refuses to see a doctor for annual checkups. He avoids mirrors when undressing. The memory of the attack is not a story he tells; it is a presence that lives in his muscles, in the way he holds himself rigid at his desk, in the way he cannot walk down a quiet street without his heart hammering.

Today, in session, he described a new trigger: a ceremonial scarf a client brought him from their homeland. The fabric is the same rough weave as the jacket one of his attackers wore. Rajesh put it in a drawer, then took it out, then put it back. He is angry at himself for being weak. He is angry at the men. He is angry at his wife for leaving. Mostly, he is tired-a bone-deep exhaustion that no sleep can remedy.

He arrives to our sessions punctually, always wearing a pressed shirt, always sitting on the edge of the chair. He speaks in measured sentences, as if every word is a stone he is placing carefully. He never cries. But sometimes, when he reaches the part about the alley, his voice goes dry, and he stares at a point on the wall behind me, and I know he is somewhere I cannot follow.
